paragraphs.title: Humility, God, and the Request for Balance

answers: He is more brutish than any man and lacks understanding
He is wiser than all kings
easy.explanation: The speaker says, “Surely I am more brutish than any man,” and that he lacks understanding.
easy.q: How does the speaker describe his understanding?

easy.explanation: The questions about heaven, wind, waters, and the earth point to God’s greatness.
easy.q: Who is presented as having greatness beyond human understanding?

easy.explanation: He asks, “Remove far from me vanity and lies.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask to have removed far from him?

answers: So that he may live rightly and avoid denying God or stealing
So that he can become famous
So that he can rule over others
medium.explanation: He asks for convenient food lest fullness lead him to deny God or poverty lead him to steal.
medium.q: Why does the speaker ask for neither poverty nor riches?

medium.explanation: The KJV presents God’s word as pure and dependable.
medium.q: What does “pure” mean in “Every word of God is pure”?

answers: He will be reproved and found a liar
medium.explanation: The verse warns, “lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.”
medium.q: What may happen to someone who adds to God’s words?

answers: Both poverty and riches can tempt a person to sin against God
Faith depends only on the amount of food one has
The request has no connection with faith
challenge.explanation: The speaker fears that riches may lead to denial and poverty may lead to stealing and taking God’s name in vain.
challenge.q: What connection does the request for balanced provision have with faithfulness to God?

answers: God’s greatness is beyond human ability to comprehend fully
challenge.explanation: The series of questions highlights God’s unmatched power and mystery.
challenge.q: What do the questions about ascending to heaven and establishing the earth emphasize?

answers: The importance of truthfulness and respecting the limits of human knowledge
The preference for power over faith
challenge.explanation: Both teachings call people to speak truthfully and avoid corrupting or pretending to improve God’s word.
challenge.q: What idea links the warning against adding to God’s words with the request to remove lies?

answers: Accusing a servant to his master
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Accuse not a servant unto his master.”
easy.q: What does the first verse in this section warn against?

answers: It curses its father and does not bless its mother
easy.explanation: The generation is said to curse its father and not bless its mother.
easy.q: How is the generation described in relation to its parents?

easy.explanation: Its teeth are compared to weapons used to devour the poor and needy.
easy.q: Whom does the generation in verse 14 devour?

answers: It is pure in its own eyes but remains unclean
It admits all of its sins
medium.explanation: The generation considers itself pure, yet it has not been washed from its filthiness.
medium.q: What contrast is shown between the generation’s self-image and its conduct?

answers: To report a charge against someone
medium.explanation: To accuse a servant is to bring a complaint or charge against him before his master.
medium.q: What does “accuse” mean in “Accuse not a servant unto his master”?

answers: Arrogance and oppression of the weak
medium.explanation: The generation has lofty eyes and uses its strength against the poor and needy.
medium.q: What repeated quality appears in the description of the generation?

answers: The servant may curse the accuser, who may then be found guilty
It prevents the servant from working
challenge.explanation: The verse warns that the servant may curse the accuser and that the accuser may be found guilty.
challenge.q: Why could accusing a servant be dangerous according to the verse?

answers: It considers itself pure but acts arrogantly and cruelly
challenge.explanation: The generation claims purity while displaying pride and preying on the vulnerable.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in the description of the generation?

answers: From dishonoring parents to false purity and pride, ending in oppression of the poor
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from cursing parents to self-righteousness, arrogance, and exploitation.
challenge.q: How does the criticism develop from verses 11 through 14?

paragraphs.title: Things That Are Never Satisfied and the Punishment for Disrespect

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The horseleach hath two daughters.”
easy.q: How many daughters does the horseleach have?

easy.explanation: They are described as crying, “Give, give.”
easy.q: What do the daughters of the horseleach cry?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother.”
easy.q: What is said to mock the father and despise obeying the mother?

medium.explanation: All four are listed as things that never say, “It is enough.”
medium.q: What do the grave, the barren womb, the earth, and the fire have in common?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes an unending appetite or demand.
medium.q: What does “never satisfied” mean in this passage?

answers: Both represent continual taking or demand
medium.explanation: The horseleach’s cry, “Give, give,” introduces the theme of insatiable desire.
medium.q: How is the horseleach related to the list of four unsatisfied things?

answers: Failure to exercise restraint and honor can lead to serious consequences
challenge.explanation: The passage warns against uncontrolled desire and contempt for parental authority.
challenge.q: What moral principle connects lack of satisfaction with disrespect for parents?

answers: To show the seriousness of despising parents
To explain how ravens are raised
challenge.explanation: The imagery of ravens and young eagles emphasizes the gravity of the offense.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the vivid punishment for the mocking eye?

answers: It expands the idea of an appetite that never stops
It removes the idea of demand
challenge.explanation: The list develops the horseleach’s repeated demand for more.
challenge.q: How does the list of never-satisfied things strengthen the picture of the horseleach?

paragraphs.title: Four Mysterious Paths and Reversed Social Order

easy.explanation: The verse says, “There be three things... yea, four which I know not.”
easy.q: How many things does the speaker call too wonderful for him?

easy.explanation: The first path is “the way of an eagle in the air.”
easy.q: Which creature’s path is described as being in the air?

easy.explanation: Verse 22 includes “a servant when he reigneth.”
easy.q: Which social situation is described as difficult for the earth to bear?

answers: They are difficult to trace or understand
They all occur on dry land
medium.explanation: The paths of the eagle, serpent, ship, and man with a maid are presented as mysterious.
medium.q: What do the four paths in verses 19 and 20 have in common?

answers: A woman who breaks marital faithfulness
A woman who sails at sea
medium.explanation: The term describes a woman who commits adultery.
medium.q: What does “an adulterous woman” refer to?

answers: Both present things that are mysterious or difficult to endure
medium.explanation: The first group is hard to understand, while the second group represents disturbing reversals of order.
medium.q: What connection exists between the four paths and the four social situations?

answers: She commits the act, wipes her mouth, and claims innocence
challenge.explanation: She eats, wipes her mouth, and says, “I have done no wickedness.”
challenge.q: What is surprising about the adulterous woman’s conduct?

answers: They overturn the expected social order
challenge.explanation: The examples describe people of low status suddenly occupying positions of authority or inheritance.
challenge.q: Why are a reigning servant and an heir maidservant presented as situations the earth cannot bear?

answers: From mysterious movement and relationships to disturbing reversals of social position
From food preparation to farming and trade
From humility to prayer and wealth
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from four mysterious ways to four unsettling social conditions.
challenge.q: What is the main progression of ideas in this section?

paragraphs.title: The Wisdom of Small Creatures and Confident Movement

easy.explanation: These four creatures are listed as little upon the earth but exceedingly wise.
easy.q: Which creatures are described as little but exceedingly wise?

easy.explanation: The ants prepare their meat in the summer.
easy.q: What do the ants prepare in the summer?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The spider taketh hold with her hands.”
easy.q: Where does the spider take hold?

answers: They prepare food ahead of time
They wait for a king to lead them
They do not work in summer
medium.explanation: Although they are not strong, the ants prepare their meat in summer.
medium.q: What does the ants’ behavior show about their wisdom?

answers: A people that does not exist
A people that is never hungry
medium.explanation: The conies are weak, yet they protect themselves by making houses in the rocks.
medium.q: What does “a feeble folk” mean in the description of the conies?

answers: They overcome weakness through useful or clever behavior
medium.explanation: The ants prepare, the conies find shelter, the locusts move together, and the spider reaches kings’ palaces.
medium.q: What do the four small creatures have in common?

answers: They go forth together in organized bands
challenge.explanation: The locusts have no king, yet they go forth together by bands.
challenge.q: How are the locusts shown to be wise even though they have no king?

answers: A small creature can reach a high and impressive place
challenge.explanation: Though small and easily caught, the spider is found in kings’ palaces.
challenge.q: What does the spider’s presence in kings’ palaces suggest?

answers: Even a king’s confidence does not remove the possibility of examining royal pride
The king is weaker than an ant
challenge.explanation: The passage’s confident creatures and king may invite reflection on the limits of human pride.
challenge.q: What possible ironic point appears in the contrast between the creatures and the king?

paragraphs.title: The Danger of Pride and Anger

answers: Lay his hand upon his mouth
easy.explanation: The verse says, “lay thine hand upon thy mouth.”
easy.q: What should a person do if he has lifted himself up or thought evil?

easy.explanation: The verse says that churning milk brings forth butter.
easy.q: What does the churning of milk bring forth?

easy.explanation: The verse concludes, “the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife.”
easy.q: What does the forcing of wrath bring forth?

answers: Pride or evil thoughts may lead to harmful speech, so restraint is needed
medium.explanation: The verse advises silence and self-control after foolish pride or evil thoughts.
medium.q: What is the connection between lifting oneself up and laying a hand upon the mouth?

answers: The pressure or escalation of anger
medium.explanation: The phrase describes anger being pressed or stirred until it produces conflict.
medium.q: What does “the forcing of wrath” describe?

medium.explanation: Wringing the nose brings forth blood, and forcing wrath brings forth strife.
medium.q: According to the verse, what can pressure and anger produce?

answers: Both show a process in which pressure produces a result
challenge.explanation: Churning produces butter, while pressure and anger produce bloodshed and strife.
challenge.q: What common structure links the images of milk and wrath?

answers: It shows that pride and evil thoughts can develop into quarrels
challenge.explanation: The conclusion connects self-exaltation and anger with destructive conflict.
challenge.q: How does the ending continue the chapter’s warnings about pride?

answers: Lay a hand upon the mouth and exercise restraint
challenge.explanation: Laying a hand upon the mouth symbolizes stopping harmful speech and controlling oneself.
challenge.q: What practical action does the verse recommend to someone who has acted foolishly or thought evil?
